title: Huerfano County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: In Huerfano County, median well depth is 113 ft with typical yields around 8 gpm. See what that means for drilling cost and water supply.
h1: Water wells in Huerfano County, Colorado
intro_html:
Huerfano County is classic fractured-bedrock mountain country, and the well records show it. Some owners hit water in a shallow hole, others have to chase fractures hundreds of feet down. Looking at the permits on file helps set expectations before you buy land or plan a new build out here.

The numbers below are pulled from Colorado Division of Water Resources data for Huerfano County wells, not averages from somewhere else. Use them as a reality check when talking to drillers and planning your budget.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Huerfano County
sections.html:
Across Huerfano County, the median total well depth is about 113 feet, but the spread is wide. Half of reported wells fall between 42 and 350 feet, and about 12% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest on record at 2,800 feet. Around 44% of wells are under 100 feet, while 19% land between 300 and 600 feet.

Most wells are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers (4,018 wells), which is why depths vary so much from one ridge or valley to the next. When you ask for bids, a driller will usually base pricing on a range that covers this middle band, then warn you that the hole may need to go deeper if the fractures are stingy.

sections.heading: Water table depth and recent trend here
sections.html:
Static water levels reported in Huerfano County show a median depth to water of 76 feet, with the middle half of measurements between 25 and 237 feet below the surface. That’s the level the water sits at in the hole when it’s at rest, not the total well depth.

By decade, the median static level has changed from about 60 feet below ground in the 2010s to about 117 feet in the 2020s. That suggests water levels are, on average, deeper in newer measurements. On a specific parcel near places like Walsenburg, La Veta, or Gardner, you’ll want to look up nearby wells by permit number and measurement date to see how your immediate area compares.

sections.heading: Well yield and how much water to expect
sections.html:
Based on reported tests, the median pump yield in Huerfano County is about 8.0 gallons per minute, with half of wells between 5.0 and 11.2 gpm. That’s generally plenty for a normal single-family household and some light outdoor use, especially under an exempt household-use permit with the usual 35 gpm pumping limit.

Most wells fall in the 5–15 gpm band (61%), and about 14% test over 15 gpm. Low producers exist: 3% of wells report under 1 gpm and 22% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. A 1–5 gpm well can still be workable with storage, but if you see yields in that range on nearby permits, plan for a conservative water-use layout and maybe bigger tanks.

sections.heading: Who is drilling here and when wells went in
sections.html:
Colorado’s records list 4,149 well permits in Huerfano County, with 2,460 marked as constructed and 2,590 reporting a total depth. Drilling picked up sharply starting in the 1970s and 1990s and has stayed active since. Permits by decade run from 11 in the 1950s and 46 in the 1960s up to 251 in the 1970s, 224 in the 1980s, 807 in the 1990s, 968 in the 2000s, 663 in the 2010s, and 339 so far in the 2020s. The newest permit year on record is 2026.

The most active drillers in the county’s history include Ojo Spring Drilling & Well Service (Blouin, Octave George) with 319 wells, Timber Line Drilling (Pfaffenhauser, Robert G.) with 289, and Authorized (Pe, Pg) with 242. When you’re shopping land, it’s worth pulling old permits to see who drilled nearby and what they hit.

sections.heading: Typical cost to drill a new well in Huerfano County
sections.html:
Here the ground is mostly fractured granite and gneiss, and drillers usually price by the foot. A typical rate runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the county’s median depth of 113 feet, that puts the drilled hole itself in the ballpark of $7,300–$11,300.

Once you include casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, a finished domestic well at that depth generally falls around $13,300–$23,300. Because the middle half of wells run from 42 to 350 feet, you need to budget for the possibility of going significantly deeper than the median, especially on higher or rockier ground.

sections.heading: Risks to check: low yield, dry holes, and contamination
sections.html:
In fractured-bedrock systems, two parcels a few hundred yards apart can have very different results. With 3% of tested wells under 1 gpm and 22% between 1 and 5 gpm, low-yield wells are a real possibility. Review nearby permits for depth and yield, and assume deeper drilling where surrounding wells are in the 300–600+ foot range.

Huerfano County also has mapped environmental concerns: 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 143 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Those don’t mean your water is bad, but they do mean you should plan on a good lab test panel on any existing well and thoughtful siting of new wells and septic systems to keep them separated.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a Huerfano County lot
sections.html:
Most Huerfano County permits are for domestic or household-type use (about 68%), with stock watering making up about 41%, some monitoring wells (12%), and a smaller share of irrigation (2%). That lines up with smaller ranches and rural homes spread across the county and into nearby areas like Las Animas, Costilla, Custer, Pueblo, and Alamosa counties.

When you evaluate a parcel, pull the DWR records for at least a half-dozen nearby wells: look at total depth, static level, and yield. Match your build site and septic location to the best drilling area on the property, not just the prettiest view. On vacant land with no well, negotiate based on the real possibility of needing a few hundred feet of hole rather than assuming the shallow 113-foot median.

faq.q: How deep are domestic water wells in Huerfano County, Colorado?
faq.a: In Huerfano County, the median well depth is about 113 feet, but the range is broad. Half of reported wells are between 42 and 350 feet deep. About 44% of wells are under 100 feet, 25% fall between 100 and 300 feet, 19% are between 300 and 600 feet, and 12% go deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest at 2,800 feet.

faq.q: What well yield can I expect in Huerfano County?
faq.a: Reported pump tests show a median yield of about 8.0 gpm in Huerfano County, with the middle half of wells between 5.0 and 11.2 gpm. Around 61% of wells fall in the 5–15 gpm range, 14% are over 15 gpm, 22% are between 1 and 5 gpm, and only about 3% are under 1 gpm. Always check nearby well reports for your specific area.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Huerfano County?
faq.a: Static water level data suggest deeper water levels in recent measurements. Overall, the median depth to water is about 76 feet, with half of readings between 25 and 237 feet. By decade, the median static level was about 60 feet below ground in the 2010s and about 117 feet in the 2020s, indicating that, on average, water levels are being found deeper in newer records.

faq.q: What does it cost to drill a water well in Huerfano County?
faq.a: Drilling in Huerfano County’s fractured bedrock typically runs about $65–$100 per foot. At the median depth of 113 feet, the borehole alone usually costs around $7,300–$11,300. A complete domestic well system with pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical commonly totals about $13,300–$23,300 at that depth. Deeper wells toward the 300–600 foot range will scale up from there.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Huerfano County, Colorado?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. The county has 8 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 143 historic mine features, and 2 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so local geology and history matter. Many homes use well water safely, but you should test a new or existing well with a certified lab and design your septic system to maintain good separation from the well.
